content: Linoleic acid, commonly abbreviated as LA, is an unsaturated omega-6 fatty acid. It exists as a colorless liquid and is chemically classified as a carboxylic acid with an 18-carbon chain and two cis double bonds. The first double bond is located at the sixth carbon from the omega end of the molecule. In scientific literature, it is often referred to as 18:2(n-6). The term linoleic is derived from the Greek word linon, meaning flax, while oleic refers to its relationship to oil or oleic acid. When the omega-6 double bond is removed, linoleic acid is converted into oleic acid. From a physiological perspective, linoleic acid is a polyunsaturated fatty acid that plays a critical role in the biosynthesis of prostaglandins, which are important signaling molecules in the body. It is a key component of the lipids found in cell membranes and is abundant in many vegetable oils, particularly safflower oil and sunflower oil. For the body to fully utilize linoleic acid, it must be enzymatically converted into gamma-linolenic acid (GLA) through a reaction catalyzed by the enzyme delta-6-desaturase (D6D). Linoleic acid belongs to the group of essential fatty acids known as omega-6 fatty acids, which are termed essential because they must be obtained through the diet as mammals cannot synthesize them. Another group of essential fatty acids is the omega-3 fatty acids, such as alpha-linolenic acid. A deficiency in omega-6 fatty acids can lead to symptoms such as dry hair, hair loss, and impaired wound healing. However, it is relatively easy to meet the daily dietary requirement for omega-6 fatty acids, even for individuals consuming low-fat diets. Most people obtain sufficient amounts of omega-6 fatty acids by consuming approximately one tablespoon of polyunsaturated plant oils per day. Linoleic acid also has industrial applications. It is used in the production of soaps, emulsifiers, and quick-drying oils. When reduced, linoleic acid yields linoleyl alcohol. In recent years, linoleic acid has gained popularity in the beauty and skincare industry due to its beneficial effects on the skin. Research has demonstrated that topical application of linoleic acid can provide anti-inflammatory effects, reduce acne, and improve moisture retention in the skin. Noni seed oil, which is rich in linoleic acid, is a common ingredient in various beauty products. Linoleic acid is found in a wide range of oils and foods. These include safflower oil (78%), poppy seed oil (70%), walnut oil, grass-fed cow milk, olive oil, palm oil, sunflower oil, soybean oil, lard, coconut oil, egg yolks (16%), spirulina, peanut oil, okra, rice bran oil, wheat germ oil, grape seed oil, macadamia oil, pistachio oil, and sesame oil.
